title: Long story - rich but not too rich dough recipe help | Houzz Forum
text: As anyone who sees my posts knows I bake for my mom fairly often.. (her easier to please partner is included too) She is not terribly happy with old age, frailty and the state of the world lately. While she is a 60 year rural Maine resident my mom grew up in a tiny jewish diaspora town in NJ and spent her early adulthood in NYC. She takes her baked goods very seriously. When her dad taught in Cambridge (ie Boston) for a year when she was in HS a family friend from Philadelphia sent her sourdough rye weekly.  Her favorite part of Maine’s foody culture is baked goods. In her old age whenever we go anywhere she is thinking about where to get a snack. The choices are markedly improved from years ago but still limited. I have been trying to make a good coffee cake for her. Ok on to the cake…. She likes crumb cakes and babkas etc… In the past year I make her the King Arthur cinnamon crisp coffee cake a few times. She liked it but mentioned how rich it is. I made several babkas - semi sucessful. Very dense and rich. The day before yesterday I had asked them to pick up some cinnamon for me. They brought me three bags. And mentioned crumb cake again. They were expecting a rare visit from beloved frail friends yesterday. So I got up early made up a yeast risen cake. I  used the chocolate filling and the cinnamon crumb from the King Arthur recipe.  I have a basic high hydration bread dough I use for focaccias.  I replaced some of the water with butter and eggs. Added some sugar. This came out really well. The crumb was soft and fluffy but not too sweet. The cinnamon cocoa filling was thin chocolatey gooey layer. The crumbs were sweet rich and cinnamony. The friends all asked to bring some home. My mom and her guy were happy and have leftovers. As do I. BUT I think the dough still was lean enough that it will fairly stale quickly. I feel like I have a handle in what I am going for now. I am very close. I need a slightly sweet dough that is rich enough to last a few days. Suggestions for a moderately rich dough?  I will experiment but with baking I tend to like to tweak a recipe rather than winging it. Note to self: Do not carry a bottle of vanilla in your back pocket. My pants smell good but that was an expensive spill.   https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/recipes/cinnamon-crisp-coffee-cake-recipe

title: Quercus laurifolia in northern VA | Houzz Forum
author_name: Dave in NoVA • N. Virginia • zone 7A
text: I ran over to the Community College nearby and took some pics of what I believe to be Quercus laurifolia (Swamp laurel oak / Diamond leaf oak / Laurel oak).  It's a fairly impressive specimen for this far north.  I know they are looked down upon in the South for their weak growth and shorter life (compared to live oak) and are sometimes referred to as 'Damn Laurel Oak'. Among the leaf characteristics that help to distinguish it from hemisphaerica are the cuneate to attenuate bases on laurifolia leaves vs the more rounded bases on hemisphaerica leaves, as well as the occasional diamond-shape leaf on laurifolia. And laurifolia rarely has any lobing on adult leaves. Also, leaf tips on laurifolia tend to be rounded, while those of hemisphaerica can be pointed with bristle tips. Acorns are small and look similar to those of Q. phellos, but maybe just a bit larger. The cap of the Q. hemisphaerica acorn tends to be flatter, and acorns more 'half-sphere' shape, than those of laurifolia (acorns of laurifolia are near-spherical in shape).  Laurel oak is in the red oak family, so it fairly easy to distinguish from Q. virginiana. I do not recall I've ever seen limb damage on these Laurel oaks from heavy ice or snow loads. Maybe that is because by the time we get most of our heavy snows, enough leaves have fallen so the snow or ice can't accumulate as readily. The leaves (especially those exposed to the sun) don't look great this year due to our very dry summer. And since this is a water-loving tree, it's not looking perfect this season.

title: Apple Pie Cookies | Houzz Forum
text: In a never-ending quest to find new and tasty cookies to bake with (or without) cannabutter, I've cobbled together this recipe. This version, by the way, is the third and definitely the best! Ingredients: 2 cups all-purpose flour - packed 1 teaspoon baking powder 1 cup crushed dehydrated apples - Costco has a huge bag of red crisps 1 teaspoon cinnamon 1/2 teaspoon cloves 1/2 teaspoon allspice 1 cup white chocolate chips 1 stick unsalted butter or 120 grams cannabutter 1/2 cup brown sugar - packed 1/2 cup white sugar 1 egg 1 tablespoon vanilla extract Process: Cream the butter and sugar. Add the egg and vanilla and mix. Combine the dry ingredients in a bowl and whisk together. Add the dry ingredients to the wet and mix well. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees and line a cookie sheet with parchment. Roll the dough into 1" balls and flatten. Bake for 20 minutes. Yields 2 dozen cookies. Note: You might need a little milk or cream to moisten the dough while still in the mixer.

title: Christmas Gifts on demand and why does ___ look like that.  Very long. | Houzz Forum
text: Part I: I work in an office and each year the staff buys the boss a Christmas gift, they buy me a small gift and I have been giving the same gift to everybody for the last 25  plus years.  I work there one day a week, and no longer work with everybody. Last year as usual I bought the identical gift for everybody, and that included two people I work with every week, one for 28 years, one for 17; the boss, who I see briefly once a month or so; a long time staff member who I saw two times the entire year; a staff member there less than a year who left immediately after the holiday; another staff member I only met once; and the boss's wife, who was insulted that the year before I included her with her husband, because she works there (rarely when I am there and she should have gotten her "own" gift because she "works there too") . Yes it's one of those workplaces. It used to be a smaller group of long-term employees who got along with each other (except maybe the boss). And now there are a couple long-term hold-outs, three of whom are more or less planning their exit strategies, a couple people in revolving door positions who are perfectly nice, but don't need this job in particular, and could leave any time they get annoyed enough, and at least one person who has poisoned the office environment, whom no one likes (staff or clientele alike) and likes no one. So my gift has gotten more and more expensive and this year I thought, "Last year I gave the same thing to two people I saw once or twice, one of whom I didn't know at all, two people who were there less than a year and left after the holiday, and one person I do not like at all. I am not doing that again" So this year has been a series of mishaps. I found a set of six perfectly nice gifts for everyone but the two people I work most closely with (and for decades). They are not as nice as I would normally give, but nice. They came without individual gift boxes. I ordered gift boxes online, and they never got delivered or they got stolen. Still dealing with that. I ordered more gift boxes. They are supposed to be here by the Thursday before Christmas and of course I would need them the Friday before at the latest. I ordered the "nicer" ornaments for the two people I work closely with from Etsy (not my usual source) . They came without boxes. They are nice looking but the size of my finger. I ordered two others. They are okay, I don't like them much, so those to people will get two things each. I don't like all that much.  I still don't have boxes. I really should have just bought the same thing for everybody, spent the same amount of money on everybody, it would have been much less of a hassle. Part II: Since I didn't get boxes (which I used to wrap creatively and in a way that the box could be used as a long-term storage box), I thought "I will just buy little gift bags" Easier said than done. I found some nice looking sturdy small gift bags. --$8 a piece--. I really don't want to spend $60 on gift bags. So I went to the Dollar Store in my neighborhood, and they had nice sturdy gift bags for $1-2 a piece. Each more hideous than the next. How is baby blue a good predominant color for a Christmas gift bag. This is the second part of my title. There is definitely a difference in printing quality between the $1 bag and the $8 bag. But they are the same thing. The manufacturing process is the same the paper weight is the same. Does the slight quality upgrade of the physical surface of the bag warrant an 8 fold price increase? But my bigger question is: "Is this bag cheaper because it is so ugly, or is it so ugly because it is cheap?" In other words is it ugly because that is what people shopping at that price point really like? Or is it just what they are stuck with. I can't help but think it would be a little bit of both. Part III: In my other workplace we do a Secret Santa/Pollyanna gift exchange, excluding the two office assistants/secretaries for whom a monetary gift is collected. I should note that for many many years, the evening office assistant who is only there a couple nights a week for a few hours each got Zip. Finally the people who worked at night said that she should get something too. And some people who worked at night only worked with her. We also pay their way when we go out twice a year as an office. Anyway, most of the people who work there now think the monetary gift for the full time daytime assistant secretary is extortion. She has never done for years much except answer the phone. With changing technology to computerized everything, she has no pulling or filing of paperwork. She does not stock supplies. She does not make copies. She used to make copies for various people, now that is officially "Not her job" and she is allowed to tell you everything is "not her job".  She answers the phone, she eats, she looks at things on the computer, she listens to radio talk shows and cackles for about 7 hours a day. She may spend about one hour a day total answering the phone or ordering supplies, if someone tells her that something is running low, it's no longer her job to check on any stock.  She assigns certain types of patients to the students, I don't really think it's an hour a day anymore. We got a friendly reminder  about the gift because I guess the contributions are not flowing in. Some texting went around that people do Not really want to give any money but we are essentially blackmailed into it. It's anonymous, but there is an envelope to put it in and it's guaranteed that the envelope gets checked and she knows exactly who put what in when. And they will be treated accordingly. She still won't do anything for anybody, but she won't be quite as rude if you pony up some cash. One person emailed back to the supervisor who sent the friendly reminder, basically telling her to get lost, she wasn't giving a gift to someone who does nothing. We'll see how that goes. The people who are there full time are all succumbing to the blackmail.

title: What are your best/favorite cookies to bake?  Do they dominate? | Houzz Forum
text: Ricky posted his new dried fruit apple pie cookie recipe recently, and it got me to thinking.  A couple of my favorite cookies are from my old loose leaf Betty Crocker cookbook, which my parents gave me when I was nine.  My all time favorite is the Moravian ginger cookies, which are molasses more than ginger, and roll out thin and crisp.  They get soggy when frozen, and are brittle enough to need to be handled with care if there are thin bits like legs, and the dough degrades with repeated rollouts, but they're ever so good.  The other ones from BC are applesauce and oatmeal.  Toll House from the old package with a spoon (half tsp. for 12oz. chips recipe) of water and baking sticks (higher melt point than butter) are fab, and I can make them well, but The Expert makes the best ones.  I know his secrets, but haven't perfected them.  For rolled and cut/stamped, my best are my Scottish nanny's shortbreads.  These last two crowd out all the others! We used to bake lots and lots of cookies, which went to all the school parties, organizations, etc.  Variety was good, but the chocolate chip and shortbread always went first.  It's such a shame!  Moravian ginger cookies are molasses brown, flat and undecorated.  They look boring but are the tastiest of all!  Applesauce are drop cookies, and not perfectly shaped, but tender and oh so good.  And while people are disappointed if they're aiming for chocolate chip and bite onto oatmeal raisin, that doesn't meam oatmeal aren't good!  So I'm wallowing in a fit of nostalgia, but have no one to bake my favorite cookies for.  —Shout out to Annie's ”cuppa” peanut butter cookies, which make hollow boxes by ”popovering” in a mini-cheesecake pan, and are delicious!  Though less peanutty than the old BC recipe with the fork grids.— The young ones eat lots of sweets, but they're disguised as ”healthy” even if structurally they're just cookies. So.  I have my ”new” cookie cutters I got last year but didn't get to use, which make pretty shapes with a well in the middle for jam or whatnot, to make faux linzers.  I think I'll pivot, however, and make a nut dough.  Maybe that'll be faux healthy enough for the young ones.

title: Unofficial Design Dilemma Boot Camp | Houzz Forum
text: Here's the best way to get good Comments. Keep in mind that you're inviting some design pros and people with a design eye into your home via photos. If they walked into your actual space, they would take in all of it: all four sides, doorways, floors, windows, ceiling, trim--the "givens"--then the features that can be changed--furnishings, paint, art, rugs, decor items, etc. It's all one first impression. Same thing with photos. That's why it's important to provide well lit photos of the entire space, taken from all sides of a room regardless of the size of your problem. 1. Post one thread for the same room so Commentors don't have to dig back or repeat their suggestions. 2. Take pictures of all four walls of an entire space.* 3. Provide measurements. 4. State the feeling and function you want for the space. (Examples: Do you regularly have a lot of company or small children or live by yourself?) 5.. Mention budget, dealbreakers, and restrictions (ex: keeping wood cabinets/big black leather sofa/recliner no matter what). 6. Define whether you're looking for approval for something already decided or whether you're open to suggestions you might not have considered. 7. Consider that the problem you've identified may not be the actual problem that outside Commentors see. *When asking about a house exterior, take shots from far away so Commentors can see setting, neighbors, then closeup about ten feet away, then very closeup of materials, specific problem, etc.

title: From Cleaning to Staining: Step-by-Step Cedar Siding Maintenance Guide | Houzz Forum
text: Discover the beauty and durability of cedar siding, a top choice for homeowners seeking exterior longevity. Learn how to properly maintain and care for your wood siding in our comprehensive guide. From cleaning to staining, we've got you covered to ensure your home stays stunning for years to come. So, let's dive in and discover the secrets to cedar siding maintenance! Cleaning Your Cedar Siding To keep your cedar siding looking its best, it is essential to clean it regularly. Dust, dirt, and debris can build up on the surface of your siding, dulling its natural color and posing a risk for mold growth. The good news is that cleaning cedar siding is relatively simple and can be done with basic household cleaners. Start by rinsing down your siding with a garden hose to remove any loose dirt and dust. Then, mix warm water in a bucket with an all-purpose cleaner or mild detergent, such as dish soap. Using a soft-bristled brush or sponge, gently scrub the siding in small sections from bottom to top. Rinse each section thoroughly before moving on to the next.Visit on Electrical walled in area for more data. For tougher stains or mold growth, use a solution of one part bleach to four parts water. Apply the mixture to the affected area, let it sit for 10-15 minutes, and then rinse thoroughly. Be careful not to oversaturate your siding with the bleach solution, as this can cause damage. Inspecting for Damages After cleaning, it's crucial to inspect your cedar siding for any damages. As a natural material, wood is susceptible to rot and insect infestation. Catching these issues early on can save you from costly repairs down the line. Here's what you should look out for: Cracks or splits in the wood These can be caused by extreme temperatures or changes in humidity. If left untreated, they can lead to further damage. Rot Wood rot occurs when moisture penetrates the wood and causes it to decay. Look out for soft spots or discoloration on your siding, as these may be signs of rot. Insect Infestations Certain insects, such as termites and carpenter ants, can wreak havoc on your cedar siding. Look for any holes or tunnels along the wood surface. Warping or Buckling This occurs when the wood siding has been exposed to excessive moisture or heat, causing it to twist or bend out of shape. Keep an eye out for boards that are not perfectly flat. Peeling Paint or Stain If the paint or stain on your cedar siding is peeling, it could be a sign that the treatment has failed and needs to be reapplied. This also exposes the wood to the elements, increasing the risk of other forms of damage. Fading Over time, sun exposure can cause the color of your cedar siding to fade. While this isn't a structural issue, it can detract from the aesthetic appeal of your home. Water Stains Dark water stains can appear if your siding is not properly sealed or if the moisture is not properly diverted away from your home. These stains can be an early indication that the siding is absorbing moisture and could lead to more serious issues like rot Staining Your Cedar Siding. Staining is an important step in maintaining your cedar siding as it helps protect the wood from weathering and UV rays. It also enhances the natural color and grain of the wood, giving it a fresh look. Here are some staining tips for your cedar siding: Choose the Right Stain Ensure you choose a stain specifically designed for outdoor wood siding. These stains not only enhance the beauty of the cedar but also provide resistance against harmful UV rays, moisture, and mildew. Preparation is Key Before you start staining, make sure the surface is clean and dry. Any dirt or moisture can interfere with the stain's penetration into the wood. Test the Stain Apply the stain to a small, hidden portion of the siding to make sure you are satisfied with the color and finish before you start. Apply with a Brush Use a high-quality brush to apply the stain. Brushes offer better control, ensuring an even application and deeper penetration into the wood grain. Work in Sections Staining cedar siding is a big task. Break it down by working in sections. This prevents the stain from drying out in the middle of the application, which can lead to overlaps and streaks. Weather Matters Avoid staining your siding in direct sunlight or on hot days as the stain can dry too quickly, preventing it from properly soaking into the wood. Also, ensure the weather will remain dry for at least 24 hours after application to allow the stain to fully dry. Apply Multiple Coats Two or more thin coats of stain offer better protection and a more even finish than a single thick coat. Be sure to let each coat dry completely before applying the next. Regular Maintenance Reapply the stain every few years, or as recommended by the stain manufacturer, to keep your cedar siding looking its best and to ensure long-lasting protection. Sealing Your Cedar Siding After staining your cedar siding, it's essential to apply a sealant to provide an extra layer of protection against weather elements. The sealant helps to lock in the stain, enhancing its longevity and adding a polished finish to your exterior. Here's a step-by-step guide to sealing your cedar siding: Choose the Right Sealant Choosing the right sealant for exterior wood siding is crucial. Look for one that resists stains, protects against the elements, and is specifically designed for outdoor use. With the right sealant, you can prolong the life and beauty of your wood siding, shielding it from moisture, UV rays, and other potential damage. Make an informed decision to keep your exterior wood siding in top shape for years to come. Prepare the Surface Before applying the sealant, it is crucial to ensure that the surface is thoroughly cleaned and completely dry. Removing any dirt, dust, or debris will help create a smooth and flawless finish. Additionally, allowing sufficient drying time will optimize the effectiveness of the sealant and ensure long-lasting protection. Taking these steps will guarantee optimal results and enhance the durability of the treated surface. Apply in Thin Coats To ensure proper application, use a high-quality brush with fine bristles to apply thin and even coats of sealant. Begin at the top of the surface and work your way down, following the natural direction of the wood grain. This technique helps to create a smooth and seamless finish, enhancing the overall appearance and protection of the wood. Let it Dry For optimal results, it is recommended to allow the sealant to fully dry for a minimum of 24 hours before considering the application of a second coat if deemed necessary. This waiting period ensures proper curing and enhances the overall effectiveness of the sealant, providing a more durable and long-lasting finish. Maintain as Needed To maintain the longevity and beauty of your cedar siding, it is important to regularly inspect it for any signs of wear or damage. In addition to this, make sure to reapply the sealant as needed, which is typically recommended every few years. By doing so, you can protect your cedar siding from the elements and ensure its continued durability and aesthetic appeal. Checking for Warping and Buckling Over time, cedar siding can warp or buckle due to changes in temperature and humidity. It's crucial to check for these signs regularly, as they can indicate underlying problems that need immediate attention. Here's what to look out for and what to do if you find any issues: Warping If you notice your siding is bent or cupped, this may be a sign of excessive moisture. In this case, it's important to address the source of the moisture and repair any damaged areas before re-staining. Buckling This occurs when the siding pulls away from its fasteners or becomes uneven. It can be caused by improper installation, moisture issues, or an inadequate number of fasteners. If you notice buckling, consult a professional to assess the cause and make necessary repairs. Yearly Maintenance Tips To ensure your cedar siding remains in top condition, it's advisable to carry out some maintenance tasks yearly. These tasks will help to preserve the beauty and durability of your siding, guaranteeing that your exterior looks stunning all year round. Here are our yearly maintenance tips: Regular Cleaning As discussed earlier, these cleaning tips are essential to maintain the beauty of your cedar siding. Aim to clean your siding at least once a year to remove dirt, grime, and mildew build-up. Annual Inspections Conduct a thorough inspection of your cedar siding at least once a year. Look for signs of damage such as cracks, rot, or insect infestations. Early detection and repair can prevent costly repairs in the future. Reapply Stain and Sealant Depending on the product used and your local weather conditions, you may need to reapply the wood stain and sealant every 2-5 years. This will keep your siding looking vibrant and provide continued protection against weathering and UV rays. Check for Warping and Buckling As a natural material, cedar siding can warp or buckle due to changes in temperature and humidity. Regular checks will allow you to spot and address these issues early. Professional Maintenance While many cedar siding maintenance tasks can be done on your own, consider hiring a professional every few years for a thorough inspection and servicing. They can spot potential issues that you might miss and provide expert wood siding care. Trim Overhanging Branches Ensure trees and bushes near your home are regularly trimmed. Overhanging branches can scratch or damage your siding and plants in direct contact with your siding can promote mildew and rot. Adjust Sprinklers If you have a sprinkler system, make sure it doesn't directly hit your cedar siding. The regular onslaught of water can cause premature weathering and potential water damage. When to Replace Your Cedar Siding Despite your best maintenance efforts, there might come a time when your cedar siding needs to be replaced. It's important to recognize the signs early to avoid more extensive and expensive damage. Let's take a look at the key signs that indicate it's time to replace your cedar siding: Extensive Rot If the wood is severely decayed and cannot be fixed, it's essential to replace the siding. Deteriorated wood can compromise your home's structure and cause additional damage. By promptly addressing this issue and installing new siding, you can ensure the long-term durability and aesthetic appeal of your property. Splitting or Cracking Excessive damage to cedar siding, including splitting, cracking, and insect infestation, may require a complete replacement. Timely replacement is crucial to preserve the durability and beauty of your property. Warping and Buckling If warping or buckling is not addressed promptly, it can lead to severe damage to your home's structure. This may compromise the structural integrity, posing safety risks and requiring expensive repairs. In some cases, complete replacement of affected components or even the entire structure may be necessary for long-term stability and functionality. Excessive Maintenance Costs Considering frequent investments in repairing and maintaining cedar siding can become costly over time, it may be financially wise to opt for a complete replacement. This not only addresses current issues but also ensures long-term cost-effectiveness and a refreshed look for your property. Hiring a Professional for Cedar Siding Maintenance Hiring a professional for cedar siding maintenance ensures thorough preservation of your exterior's beauty and longevity. They have the expertise, tools, and knowledge to clean, inspect, and treat your siding effectively. Early issue identification, expert care advice, and proper application of treatments like stains and sealants can save you time, effort, and money in the long run. An example is these cedar restoration services in Wellington for expert care and maintenance of your cedar siding. Don't compromise on the quality and durability of your property; hire a professional today! Importance of Regular Cedar Siding Maintenance Regular cedar siding maintenance is crucial for preserving your home's exterior and ensuring its long-term durability. By regularly cleaning, staining, sealing, and inspecting for damage, you can effectively safeguard the charm and integrity of your property. Investing in proper maintenance not only protects your home from potentially costly repairs or replacements but also enhances its curb appeal, leaving a lasting impression on visitors and passersby. title: (OT) Happy holidays! | Houzz Forum
text: Dear fellow forum members, This is to wish you all a happy festive season, whatever your religion or lack of it may be.  Peace, kindness, moderate jollity, and some help to those in need. This is a forum about roses, but I don't have much to say about them as it's close to the solstice and dry to boot.  Not much of a chance for roses to strut their stuff.  I have spent a part of the fall planting hedge plants, many bought from our local nursery, others that I propagated, along with a handful of other shrubs and a few trees.  We've also just started a new handkerchief-sized wood.  We have been kind of busy with various things this fall, and with drought back with us again, I've been reluctant to go wild with putting things in the ground and expecting them to grow.  It's not normal to water in December!  But, climate change.  It does offer the meager advantage of more sunny days than we used to get in the winter, with consequent improvement to my tendency to seasonal depression.  So a little good, if not much. Recently I've turned from planting to digging out some colonies of Bermuda grass that have gotten settled in the beds, unfortunately.  And there's a small patch of Johnson grass, which is even worse.  However the soil in the beds is getting better. I've mentioned in earlier posts of 2023 that I've been struggling with long Covid, a moderate form, which is bad enough.  After a year of running to the doctor, tests, exams, therapies, special diet, and the simple passage of time, I think I may finally be recovering.  I'm thankful for that, and also for many other graces this year. You folks take care. Melissa

Woah, lots of beautiful window, and I'm sure we'll be impressed. But does it lack form/proportionality? Will it feel unbalanced and overwhelming? What are your thoughts? As an alternative, I also show the same basic window coverage using three mulled 37Wx63H windows in the living area, and five of the same window in the master suite. This is pretty close to the 1:1.618 golden ratio for the individual window rectangles, for what it's worth. It does lose some of the openness of the big 57W windows, but is the form worth the tradeoff? I have been in plenty of homes with 36W individual windows and they certainly don't have any wow factor like a 57W would. But maybe three or more mulled together will? Anyways, hope this gets the point across. I'm an amateur here and just looking to avoid any major mis-steps before I go too far down any path. title: Linear shower drain gets funky after 2 weeks? | Houzz Forum
text: I'm unsure if this is a one-off or if it's standard, but we have a linear drain in our shower.  It consists of the metal trough, a metal grate on top, and in the actual drain hole that connects to the PVC pipe, there's a little basket that is there to collect anything that makes it past the metal grid.  I'm finding that after about 2 weeks, everything starts to smell musty, and the little basket clogs.  This involves pulling the tightly fitted grate out (the tool that came with it was worthless, but I picked up a trampoline spring hook on amazon that works amazing for this task), wiping the gunk out of the basket with some toilet paper, and scrubbing and rinsing the channel and the underside of the grate before reassembling it. If this is standard with linear drains, then it is what it is, and I'll get used to it, but with previous "standard" drains I've never had this much maintenance, simply clear hair that collects on top of the grate and you're good.  It certainly doesn't help that I have long hair, but as far as I can tell, the stuff that is collecting in the little basket doesn't have a lot of my long hair in it, most collects on top of the drain grid and gets picked up when the floor/walls get squeegeed after showers.  Is there something that we can do to reduce the amount of maintenance?  I've considered getting rid of that basket as I suspect it's the biggest culprit in the smell (and is not present in a normal drain) , but I'm worried that it may cause clogs in our pipes in the long term and we are on septic, so I prefer not to use drain cleaners if we can avoid it.

title: Granite quality question | Houzz Forum
text: The last couple of months I have been on the hunt for a granite countertop & fabricator. The first fabricator I obtained a quote works with a large granite wholesaler which I visited and obtained a couple of samples. The granite I like is called Pitaya white. The granite display slab and also the inventory slabs all have diagonal veining. At the suggestion of a neighbor I visited a second fabricator who happened to have a Pitaya slab in their own inventory. I looked at the slab and liked it way more more than the wholesaler's slabs as the veining is horizontal. The salesperson wanted to make clear to me that they had several customers in the past they were very unhappy with this granite as water would be spilled on the countertop and it would take several hours for the staining to disappear and the stone to dry up. They did not have any samples available. I went home and decided to do a water test on the samples I got from the wholesaler (first place). I poured several drops of water to both samples. On the first sample I let the water sit for half an hour after which I wiped it off and there was no staining on the stone whatsoever. On the second sample I let the water sit for 9 hours after which I wiped it off. There was a faint water stain that disappeared completely after 10 minutes. I would rather buy the slab from the second fabricator due to the veining but I am really troubled by what the salesperson mentioned. My question is: what could account for this difference in water staining? Quality of granite (different bundles)? Polishing techniques? Fabricator sealant? UPDATE: I tested the samples I got with olive oil, vinegar, ketchup, red wine and water. The samples from the fabricator were unsealed I learned later. I left them them for 18 hours and then wiped the granite clean, even washed it with soap water. The olive oil left a huge stain, the red wine left a faint pink stain and the vinegar you can barely see the stain. The rest of them did not leave any type of mark. I threw out the sample about a month after and the stains were still there although I tried to wash them out again.  I decided to buy the Pitaya white granite from the first fabricator and installed it in my kitchen. The second fabricator let me know that they do not seal their granites and I suspect many of their customers didn't seal their stone on their own (or call a professional) and this is the reason their granite  stained so easily. I have my countertop now for 10 months and it's amazing (it is sealed of course). It hasn't stained at all even though I cook all the time (but I wipe it when I see stains and every night). I am so impressed with this granite.

title: Wind scattered my leaf pile | Houzz Forum
text: So next time I'll bag them, put them at the curb and buy mulch from the garden center.  I have no construction skills nor tools, old pallets look awful and I can't afford to buy bins.  Have you heard something similar from beginning composters?  Those up front complaints make it difficult getting folks interested.   The surrounding 2k - 5k population towns have two dates per year when residents can bring bulk items in for free disposal,only option remainder of year is take to a for profit landfill.  I've been on a minor campaign to recruit voices for council meetings and only voices enthusiastic about recycling are going to show up and/or talk to neighbors.   Three years ago I began introducing folks to a method for handling leaves which overcome complaints mentioned.  I have been pleasantly surprised by not only good reports but people doing it on advice of a neighbor.  The key element is widely available in Eastern states and I'm sure other states have suitable substitutions.   Flat ,feather shaped Eastern Red Cedar limbs do an excellent job of holding leaves ,are easy to pull aside for making additions to pile while appearance is not near objectable as majority of budget bins.  Even after leaves have rotted limbs and twigs larger than a pencil are not rotted but remain intact making it easy to pull them out.  Some say Cedar is not suitable for compost and a few claim it can be detrimental.  Cedar shavings are very popular for horse stalls and scores of people swear by those composted stall cleanings.  Besides that, as a % the amount of Cedar is very small in finished leaves.  I hope this helps some of you that find yourself with leaves and no where to put them or that don't like the appearance of pallet bins.

title: Interesting factoids about Agatha Christie | Houzz Forum
text: Deeply hurt by the death of her mother, thirty-five-year-old Agatha Christie was still trying to overcome her grief when her husband of twelve years suddenly announced that he was in love with another woman and wanted a divorce. The twin shocks threw Agatha into a deep state of depression. Feeling that the best of life was behind her, she saw little reason to go on living. Only concern for her seven-year-old daughter saved her from suicide.Born into an affluent English family in 1890, Agatha Miller was a precocious child who taught herself to read at age four and quickly developed what would be a lifelong devotion to books. At age 22 she met Archie Christie, a dashing young pilot. The couple fell in love and were married on Christmas Eve in 1914. They spent most of the next four years separated by World War I, settling afterwards in London. Their only child, Rosalind, was born in 1919. By the time her marriage to Archie fell apart, Agatha had published five well-received detective novels, but she could hardly have expected the success that awaited her.In time Agatha began to recover from the pain of her failed marriage. She resumed writing and, to boost her spirits, took a trip on the Orient Express. Then, in 1930 a friend invited her to come along on a trip to an archeological dig in Iraq. There she met Max Mallowan, a prominent archeologist thirteen years her junior. They fell in love and were married later that year, a happy marriage that would last until Agatha’s death 46 years later.At the end of 1926, Agatha Christie may have thought that her life was no longer worth living, but she was entirely wrong about that. In the years that followed she not only found the love of her life, but she also enjoyed her greatest success, becoming the best-loved author on earth, with over 70 best-selling novels as well as the longest-running play in history. Her husband Max was knighted in 1968 and three years later Agatha was made a Dame of the British Empire.Agatha Mary Clarissa Miller Christie Mallowan died at age 85 on January 12, 1976, forty-six years ago today. title: OT - good news and bad news about our Holiday season... | Houzz Forum
text: My DH and I have been having an "interesting" (as in the old Chinese curse) holiday season so far. Remarkably, it has worked out fairly well...Hope you don't mind this not-quite-a-vent/rant. Christmas is a big deal for us, and all of our various extended families on all sides, all of whom live within 15 min to 1 1/2 hours from our house. First, on Dec 8th my DH came down with Covid for the first time ever. Of course, by Dec 10th I also tested positive. Got Plaxlovid within a couple of hours thanks to the efficiency of our doctor and pharmacy. Thought we would be better by the time of our first extended families Christmas party on Dec 23rd (11 people at my niece's), and of course fine by the one we were to host here on Christmas Eve (10 people), and then Christmas day dinner at my sister-in-law's (20 people). So, we kept on decorating, getting presents, wrapping presents, etc. By Dec 18th we were fine, and had both tested negative - Yay!. However...by Dec 20th it came back, and we were both sick again and testing positive. By that time, we had put the last ribbon on the last present,  were totally finished decorating our house, had even put the tablecloth on our large dinner table, and halfway thawed the turkey I was going to cook for the 24th. So, decided to make lemonade from our lemons, and just hunker down and enjoy the football games, our decorated house, and be cosy together with our cat in front of the fire. We got our presents for everyone at the parties on the 23rd and 25th delivered to those parties days before (lots of older teen and early 20 great nephews and nieces on both sides of our family come in handy - they are so energetic!). We re-scheduled our party here from the 24th to Jan 6th with everyone's cooperation. I cooked the turkey as planned on the 24th (it is delicious!), and have not had to cook since, of course. We had a wonderful Christmas day resting and watching football games. All great except of course the 49er game on Christmas Evening, which was a tragedy or farce, depending on how you look at it. Then...our furnace gave out completely Christmas night. All three of us were snuggled together on our bed, and totally comfortable.  Not dangerous - thank heavens we live in a mild climate, and the night time temps are around the low to mid 50s F right now. It would be damp and chilly in the house after a week (see below), however.  Built more fires in the huge fireplace. Called our plumber, who is of course on vacation until Jan 2. Called another plumber, who came and looked at it, and says we need a new furnace for $12K. My DH thinks this is correct, but we are going to hold out until our plumber of 30 years gets back in town, and get advice from him. My DH's family, including him, never throw anything that "might be useful some day" away (German AND Scots ancestry), but store whatever that is in their basements. My DH rummaged around in our basement and found 2 old ("still perfectly good") electric baseboard heaters , which he is installing upstairs as we speak. While the plumber was here I went for a 7,000 step walk around town with a friend, and it was crisp but sunny and a beautiful day. We now, of course, feel totally fine and have tested negative again. I walked all over the garden and admired all of the tea roses, all of which have a few new blooms on them. So does Schmidt's Smooth Yellow, all three bushes. So, I think I will remember this year's Christmas season with much affection - all but the 49er game, of course. Jackie

title: Rubber tree yellowing and dropping leaves | Houzz Forum
text: My beautiful 3 foot rubber tree is rapidly dropping leaves after doing well for 1.5 years.   When I got it, it was quite rootbound, and I waited too long to re-pot and it lost a few lower leaves in that time, so it was already leggy. After trimming the roots and re-potting into a larger pot, and feeding regularly, it was doing great for quite a while. I went on vacation two weeks ago and noticed one yellowing leaf. I thought perhaps it was getting a little too much water for the winter months so I didn't water it before I left. When I came back a week later, it had lost 3 more yellowed leaves and looked droopy. I checked the soil and found it to be bone-dry, so I gave it a thorough watering. Since then, it's lost another 2 leaves (that's 6 leaves in 2 weeks). All the dropping leaves have started yellowing in the center vein and stem, with yellow spreading outward through the rest of the leaf.     At this point I can't tell if the leaves are yellowing and dropping from too much water, or too little. The plant sits about 5 feet from a southwest facing window. It gets mostly indirect light, with about 2 hours of direct afternoon light this time of year (I live in New England). I had been watering it about every three weeks and I always water until water comes out of the drainage hole. The room it's in is about 68-70 during the day, 60 at night. I don't have a humidifier so it's a bit dry. The soil is a chunky mix I made myself with one part perlite, one part bark fines, and one part "potting soil".   What's baffling is that even with all these dropping leaves, there is still new growth coming in at the top. And, when I checked the soil after coming back from vacation, I felt a couple roots starting to come out of the bottom of the pot. Could it need re-potting again after only a year?   Could someone help me save this plant? If it loses any more lower leaves it's going to look quite sad, I know they won't regrow at the bottom of the plant. :(

title: How can I imitate Diane's fertilizing regime? | Houzz Forum
text: Diane,we all see your photos of your totally fantastically well-grown, beautiful roses. I just finished looking at a post of yours on portlandmysteryroses's thread on The Prince,re-reading your fertilizing regime. How I would love to be able to copy it! but, alas, here in Italy the products you mention are not available, what's more I have to be very, very careful about using organic fertilizers-no blood, bone or fish based things (they attract the very dstructive badgers). Still, I wonder if I can't find some way of approximating your routine,using a combination of substitutes. Here's a quote from Diane: " my roses get the same regimen: lots of water, a wonderful compost I  buy (Nu Life Organic compost, if you can find it; it's a regional  product), applied in late fall and into winter when the weather permits.  I'm still applying it. In late February, every rose gets a good feeding  of Plant Tone or Holly Tone, whichever I have on hand, and in mid  March, the roses get a feeding of Lilly Miller Organic granular  fertilizer for acid loving plants. My soil is alkaline so I give this  fertilizer for that reason.  My roses don't get a lot after the spring feedings. "   So what could I use as substitutes for the three products mentioned: Nu Life Organic compost, Plant/Holly Tone , and Lily Miller organic granular for acid-loving plants? The idea of fertilizing in fall and winter really resonates with me, since roses here never go really dormant in winter; I'm pretty sure that this is when they are doing almost all of their work on roots. In spring, alas, it gets too hot too early on, and in summer, forget it (that is when they get close to true dormancy, lol) . My soil is on the alkaline side, too, so the use of acid-lovers fert seems right as well. But since I have to use  non-organic chemical ferts that are locally available, how could I approximate Diane's routine? I looked up Nu Life compost 's ingredients:" Aged, screened  bark fines, composted leaf, composted steer, composted chicken, Mushroom  compost, Sphagnum peat moss and custom blend of Mycorrhizae." I'm hoping that "composted chicken" and "composted steer" means the manure from these animals, not the actual animals!  Plant Tone; Internet says: Derived from: "Hydrolyzed  Feather Meal, Pasteurized Poultry Manure, Bone Meal, Alfalfa Meal,  Greensand, Humates, Sulfate of Potash, and Sulfate of Potash Magnesia. *Contains 3.0% Slow Release Nitrogen." Poultry manure and alfalfa meal I can probably substitute with the regular manure that I buy and alfalfa hay horse fodder (with molasses in it). I can look up the other ingredients, too-the only one that is off the table for me is the blood meal. Also, I doubt I could find hydrolized feather meal over here, lol. I couldn't find an ingredients list for the Lilly Miller fert. Okay. So. I wonder if anyone out there with a mind more organized than is my own could help me figure out a way to integrate this information,help me make a DIY imitation of these products, integrated with the locally available chemical granular Nitrophoska (contains nitrogen sulfate of potash, phosphorus,sulphur, magnesium and micro elements) I do try to always add alfalfa hay, manure ,and cracked corn during fall and winter, but might it be better to compost them first, or something? title: Baked Ziti for New Year’s Day | Houzz Forum
text: Just made the sauce for this version of baked pasta my family likes.  The original recipe came from Allrecipes but I did some tweaking.  I’m posting the original recipe at the end here.  You need a fairly deep dish for this.  The one I use is 9x13 and almost 3” deep.  If you don’t have a deep dish, use less pasta (about 12 oz.) keeping the layers of it ”flatter.”  This takes less time than it looks, especially if you make the sauce a couple days in advance. Baked Ziti 2 jars marinara sauce (I use Rao’s, 22 oz. each) 1 lb. ground beef 1/2 lb. Italian sausage (mild or spicy) 1 small onion, chopped 2 cloves garlic, chopped 1/2 tsp. dried oregano 1/2 tsp. dried basil 1/4 tsp. red pepper flakes (or to taste) Red wine to rinse out marinara jars 1 lb. ziti, rigatoni, penne or pasta of choice 6 oz. Provolone cheese, sliced 1 1/2 cups sour cream 8 oz. Mozzarella cheese (I use fresh and slice it; grated is also fine.) About 1/2 cup-ish freshly grated Parmesan cheese Brown ground beef and sausage in large pot (I use a potato masher to ”crumble” the meat.).  Season with salt/pepper.  Push meat to side and add onion.  Cook for a few minutes, then add garlic, oregano, basil, pepper flakes.  Cook for another minute. Mix in marinara, rinsing both jars with about 1/4 cup each red wine (or water).  Stir into sauce.  Partially cover and simmer on low for about 30 minutes. Cook pasta about 1-2 minutes less than package directs.  You want it just undercooked (very al dente).  Drain. To Assemble: Preheat oven to 350. Grease a 9x13 DEEP baking dish.  Cover bottom of pan with thin/sparse layer of sauce.  Layer as follows: Half of pasta All of Provolone All of sour cream Half of sauce Sprinkle with Parmesan (to taste) Rest of pasta All of Mozzarella Rest of sauce (should completely cover) Top with Parmesan (to taste) Cover/tent loosely with foil.  Bake about 45-50 minutes or until bubbling. Original recipe from Allrecipes… https://www.allrecipes.com/recipe/11758/baked-ziti-i/

title: Best Reads of 2023 | Houzz Forum
text: This is my first time starting a thread, so hopefully it will work. What were your best reads of 2023? I couldn't get down to just one book, so here's the list I came up with: West With Giraffes, by Lynda Rutledge It took me a while to warm up to this book, but in the end I really, really liked it.  Set in 1938 and based on a true event:  the acquisition of 2 young giraffes by the then new San Diego Zoo.  The setting is well rendered – the Depression, Dust Bowl, Jim Crow South, the coming war—as the giraffes are trucked across the US from New York to San Diego.  The settings change with the journey, the story held together by the 3 people in the truck who try to keep the giraffes alive (driver, zoo employee, aspiring journalist) as they meet new people in each town they pass through.   Cover blurb quite accurately captures it: Part adventure, part historical saga, and part coming-of-age love story, WWG explores what it means to be changed by the grace of animals, the kindness of strangers, the passing of time.. Foster, by Claire Keegan Simple first-person narrative of a young girl (about 10 y/o)who is sent to stay with another couple for the last few months of her mother’s latest pregnancy and is returned home once the baby is born.  Written from within the girl’s POV, the story must be teased out by the reader – the craft displayed in this beautifully-written narrative is phenomenal – how much you end up knowing about the girl, her family and the husband-wife caring for her, without ever being told a thing other than the little girl’s childishly unaware observations. Some Desperate Glory by Emily Tesh This is the fun one on my list!  A wild ride of a space opera with really cool ideas of alternate realities, black hole space and AI’s, but also with depth to the characters and events that make you stop and think.  The POV character is an arrogant, unlikeable young woman who discovers that she’s been fed a load of crap by a fascist regime – this takes a lot of growing-up for a 17-y/o to realize and accept; on top of having to learn that the destruction of humanity’s Earth was actually a ‘best-outcome-for-the-many’ within the wider system of linked space-faring civilizations, due to humanity’s aggressiveness.  Makes you the reader think too! The Last Days of Ptolemy Grey  by Walter Mosley Not particularly comfortable for me to read, nor particularly uplifting, but told so well that you are immersed in the not-always-happy black African-American experience of Ptolemy’s life.  You see the story only from within the main character of Ptolemy (much like Foster, above), an elderly black man fading into dementia who is given the opportunity to reverse his dementia at the price of a drastically-shortened life.  An interesting exploration of the priorities that drive our decisions and what trade-offs we will make to achieve our goals.

title: Can anyone provide insights integration process of recruitment tools? | Houzz Forum
text: The integration process of recruitment tools with HR systems involves seamless alignment to optimize talent acquisition and management workflows. Initially, a thorough analysis of existing HR systems and recruitment tool functionalities is essential. This includes evaluating data structures, communication protocols, and security measures. Once compatibility is ensured, the integration process typically begins with establishing a secure connection between the two systems. Data mapping is crucial, ensuring that information from recruitment tools, such as candidate profiles and application status, aligns accurately with corresponding HR system fields. APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) play a pivotal role in facilitating communication between systems. Customization may be necessary to accommodate specific organizational requirements. Continuous testing is imperative to identify and rectify potential issues, ensuring a smooth data flow. User training is essential to familiarize HR teams with the integrated system. Post-implementation, ongoing support and maintenance are critical for adapting to evolving needs and technology updates. Successful integration enhances overall efficiency, providing HR professionals with a consolidated platform for streamlined recruitment and workforce management.

title: Architect designs failed zoning review - how should we respond? | Houzz Forum
text: We live on a corner lot and have spent the last two years working on an addition design that faces the street side of our home (not the front entry, the garage side). We moved out in early December, with plans for demo to take place in mid-December. Design plans for code review had been submitted in early November. Just prior to the Christmas holiday we learned our plans did not comply with zoning ordinances. The issue is that the city defines unpermissable demolition as "razing, tearing down, or demolishing a street facing wall." This is the wall that would need to be taken down to accommodate the new addition. After a great deal of obfuscation and confusion, we learned that the zoning denial was related to this definition, of which our design team was unaware. The team contends that this is an "interpretation" by the city - but the language is just as I wrote above, not ambiguous - the demolition of a street-facing wall is considered a full tear down. Further complicating the situation - if our team *had* understood the code, and gone through a conditional use permit request to allow for the demolition - the resulting build would fall under "new construction" which kicks off an entirely new set of zoning requirements to which our designs do not comply. Our question is: How severe of an oversight was the misunderstanding of "demolition" by our design team? They claim that they "learn the code by experience and this is the first time they have encountered this issue". Bear in mind that this is a leading firm with price points to match that reputation. In my research to understand what happened (the designer's explanation was insufficient for us to comprehend what had taken place), the language of the code is not only unambiguous - it is the lead paragraph on the section dedicated to demolition. The designer's contention is that the city didn't flag the zoning error in earlier conversations (which, I believe were related to confirming setbacks) and that the city's "interpretation" of the code is the source of the problem. I'd appreciate your feedback on whether this is just "one of those things" or if it exceeds the acceptable bounds of professional practice.

title: Experiments and Orders | Houzz Forum
text: Good afternoon everyone! I thought I would share a little bit of plant cheer especially for us Northerners as we approach the depths of winter. Always forging ahead, bucking conventional "wisdom", I also have some plant thrills to share.My Impatients are an autumn rescue from my old garden in 2021 and need repotting again, the Phalaenopsis is opening blooms on a new stalk after the old fades, and a third old stalk is attempting to branch again as well. It's going on 8 years old, and will soon be in bloom most of the year. The aloe is going bananas and needs potted up. My pineapple top I rooted is still trucking along and getting ever more serrated. The poinsettia is one I kept from a year ago Christmas. Shame on me, but it's still in its same container and mix. I never fertilized it. Never regulated it's daylight or darkness hours. And yet... It still coloured up before December 15th.I'm working on my second, and most likely final order of 2024, and it will be from Roses Unlimited. I've agonized over my final selections to stay in budget, but a few are for sure: Alchymist, Mirandy, Sutter's Gold, Souvenir d'Alphonse Lavallee, and Starfire. Florence Delattre is most likely another finalized selection. I was disappointed that Charlotte Armstrong, Étoile de Hollande (bush form, as noted by the lack of "Cl"), King's Ransom, and a few others aren't listed this year! Mid-Century Moderns are my weakness.Now, for the thrills! Bucking all things I have heard regarding having roses indoors as they are outdoor animals, I am keeping two potted roses in my heated basement that used to be a finished living room over the winter. Since I put up a better grow light that a buddy of mine used to grow cannabis (Michigan, don'tcha know!), they haven't just survived since October, but don't seem to be hating it and struggling, either. They are located near two windows, the electric baseboard heater, across the room from the LP forced air heat, and with a dehumidifier set to 40%. They are Mrs. Sam McGredy and Lady Emma Hamilton. LEH has a bud that has been developing since shortly before Christmas and is about fully open, smelling as divinely as she should. Mrs. Sam though not setting buds, as I expect it not to, has pushed all kinds of new growth with beautiful, healthy leaves. No bugs, no mildew, no crisping and shrivelling. I do partly suspect she may be the climbing version because she was from Rogue Valley Roses and even in full sunlight outdoor she started throwing awfully long canes but does bloom on new wood. If anyone happens to have experience with this lovely Pernetiana, I would love to hear about it.Have I somehow discovered a magic spec combination that the roses do not hate? I am planning on adding another grow light but have been pleasantly surprised at the decent progress and not to mere survival I've observed since I have brought them indoors in October!Happy gardening and cheers to being different,Steven

title: Home Renovation: A Warning About Choosing the Wrong Contractor | Houzz Forum
text: Last year, we had planned to renovate the bathrooms in our house. Amidst a booming housing market, finding skilled renovation professionals was tough. Through a friend, I met a contractor, George Zhang (Lic#: 1061182), and visited a few of his ongoing projects which seemed decent from the outside. So, we decided to hire his company for the renovation work. The demolition phase went quickly, but soon after that, issues arose. George Zhang reported outdated plumbing and suggested complete replacement. Trusting his 'expert' advice, we agreed. However, as work progressed, particularly with visible installations, numerous problems emerged. Wrong heights for washbasins, non-compliant drain installations, reversed exhaust fans, and even hot and cold water lines were mixed up. The list goes on. When confronted, George Zhang agreed to improvements but always found excuses not to follow through. We paid over $40k for labor after three bathrooms were completed. But soon, we discovered cracks near the windows in the bathrooms. On inspection, we realized that the supporting beams around the windows were improperly installed, leading to these cracks. After much negotiation, George Zhang agreed to redo the work. However, the repairs caused irreparable damage to the interior tiles. A shocking discovery was the 'dotting' technique used for tiling – less than 30% of the tile surfaces had adhesive, posing risks of tiles falling off and mold growth due to moisture seepage. Despite multiple discussions, George Zhang refused to redo the tiling and only offered repairs if problems arose. This completely shattered our confidence in his work. We terminated the contract, asking for a refund and compensation for redoing parts of the project, which he refused. We had to hire another team to redo the bathrooms, revealing more substandard work hidden beneath the surface – damaged wooden boards under the bathtub, improperly connected exhaust ducts, and poorly structured beams affecting load-bearing. This renovation taught us a hard lesson about the consequences of choosing the wrong contractor. Not only did we lose a significant amount of money, but we also endured stress and wasted time. I hope our experience serves as a warning. Be cautious with your choices; don't repeat our mistake. #RenovationHorror #ContractorWarning #HomeImprovementFail

title: "Can We Talk?" about Nonsense.... | Houzz Forum

text: Hello, we are in the middle of redoing a bathroom - it was fitted in 1980, so the time had come! We have been happy with everything so far… except the large format tiles we chose have now been fitted, and there is bowing. When I met with the tiler in advance, I said the tiles could not be more than 30% offset - because the tile manufacturer stated this, and so I had to do some research, and I understood they could only be laid about 30% past the end of the tile under and over, because manufacturing porcelain large format tiles causes some slight curve.  He said, ‘I know, one third.’  But my mistake was not getting this in writing. The tiles were laid instead like bricks, or 50% offset, and, as the manufacturer warned, this might cause some bowing. I am attaching some photos.  Is this a bad tiling job that needs to be fixed by pulling the tiles off and starting again? The tiler has said he will not redo the tile, so this would be at our expense.  He is contesting being told about the offset, but of course, this was my only reason I wanted to meet with him. When we met, he was pretty patronising.  He smiled and told me he knew how to do this job, he had tiled hundreds of bathrooms, etc. The tiler was hired by our bathroom contractor, and his fee was included in our quote, and we are paying our contractor.  The contractor also did not meet with the tiler, or approve this work in advance.  He says he expected us - the client - to ‘manage’ the tiler - whom we don’t know, and we never agreed to this. When the rain stopped I went outside to look around and at first I thought the damage was minor...a few medium sized limbs down,  lots of twigs and small stuff,   plastic tub blown a ways.   Then I went into the back yard and a very tall Leyland Cypress had crashed into our house.  I didn't even hear it.  Neither did my husband.   I mean,  it is leaning against the house but I don't think it has  damaged it much.  The smaller branches  are keeping the trunk off of the house.    I hope they get it off our house before the small branches break. Three other Leyland Cypresses lower in my garden are leaning.   On two of them the soil is raised a couple of feet with the roots  almost  out of the ground.  One is leaning towards the street.   We called the town,  a tree service,  and our insurance and all will be out here today.   I planted all those Leylands many years ago thinking they were shrubs.  They ended up very tall trees.   I am not good at  estimating feet but they look like they're 60 or 70'  tall.   We had  8 removed last year but left a few for a little privacy. The tree guys last year said that by far the most of their business involves cutting down Leyland Cypresses.   They are  shallow rooted and not long lived and they get very tall.   For years I  appreciated mine as they  provided privacy and  nice evergreen  border for my garden.   Removing 8 of them last year let in a lot more light so there was that.   Anyway,  I hope you will think twice about planting this kind of tree anywhere near your house.

I suspect this is great for the calves' health and happiness, but it used to infuriate me:  the deep hoofprints they dig into wet clay paths, and the damage they do stumbling over low slopes and through shrubs, and their occasional experimental plant sampling.  However, it eventually occurred to me that cows eat mainly grass, and that they were both mowing and fertilizing the garden.  So I became more accepting.  And it is pleasant to see livestock living free for a while and enjoying themselves. January has not been tremendously cheery here.  I caught a cold/virus/something shortly before Christmas which I haven't yet shaken off, while DH and DD are both tired, coldish, and generally feeling vaguely poorly.  The weather has been nasty for quite a while, first gray, then raining, now rawly cold, as we wimpy residents of this part of the world define cold.  The rain, though it kept us somnolent in the house, was fabulous as far as precipitation is concerned.  It rained!  Possibly two inches, though I didn't measure it.  I don't know what it did for groundwater levels, but the garden certainly got watered. I get out when the weather permits and do cleanup in the garden; also, in spite of my oft-repeated resolve never to plant after the start of the new year, DH and I have planted a few things.  I had DH dig up some starts of flowering ash and oak seedlings to plant in an open area that I want to turn into a pocket woodland.  This casual effort may not work:  if it doesn't, try again with more preparation next time.  I've continued my interminable hedging with a few plants, more to get them out of their pots, where I have to protect them from cold, than from eagerness to have them in the ground.  It's pleasant, as always, to see how the roses are doing and greet them as I work on them. There's a little in bloom:  the native Helleborus foetidus is opening its lime-green flowers; and the green snowdrops (Galanthus woronowii) in the woods are up and showing their buds.  I like the green snowdrops, but they're not what I ordered, which was the native snowdrop, G. nivalis.  I wanted native flowers for the woods, but had planted them all over before I discovered they were the wrong species.  They're spreading like mad, too.  Oh, well.  I'm still waiting for the common snowdrops, which I do have some of, to show, and their double forms:  they should bloom in January, too.

title: Residential make up air system | Houzz Forum
text: Coming here to vent, but hopefully find some answers. I am floored by how difficult it has been to find asnwers/solutions from the pros in my area. Major/multiple room renovation and this is literally the only thing that has been a significant challenge as my own GC for the project. I purchased a 36" monogram 6 burner rangetop. Has roughly 120,000 BTU output. Using calcs I have found (dividing by 100) tells me I need a 1200 CFM of exhaust. Cool. Fantech has that, not a problem. In comes MUA. The bane of my existence. Fantech has that too, with heat. I can install both in my large attic. Easy. Well not according to an HVAC engineer I spoke with. Despite my request to throw it in the attic, I am constantly being reminded that it has to be conditioned (not just heat, but also cooled) per code. I am semi calling bullsh*t. Maybe this is a commercial thing, but I haven't seen anything saying it need to be cooled. His bid??? $20k. I about defecated myself. He wants to divert the intake into the return to condition the air. I like the idea, and have seen that thrown around a bit in my research, but not 20 freaking thousand dollars. I bought a $3k range and your telling me I have to spend 7x that to have it meet code. How can someone bid a job like this that high? He must be pulling in $1k per hour. I picked the wrong field. Oh, and please dont tell me thats normal, because its not, so we can end that discussion before it starts. Anyway. I have spoke with a couple HVAC contractors as well (not engineers) and they all seem kind of shocked that I want to do this. I asked one of them how often do they put MUA in residential homes, and the answer was basically never. This guy said he was on the board that helps make the code (or something like that) in my state. There are roughly/probably 10 brands that sell these higher output ranges, marketed to residential kitchens and its impossible to find someone to install MUA. Shame on the distributors for not having an easy system or referall source for MUA, because mine sure didnt. Is this just going completely unnoticed? I mean, IT IS actually a health hazard. Dont tell me to open a window either. That doesnt meet code, but I will do that anyways. I even bought a heat pump water heater to help avoid backdrafting. I have a vented gas fireplace, and a gas furnace. Whats a guy to do? I have 2 HVAC contractors coming out in the next week. Maybe I can convince them to just install the damn inline fan and MUA in the attic without charging an arm and a leg. I know that you can place a restriction or limiter on some of these MUA systems where it can only run at so many cfm to stay below code. Thats been suggested by the guy on "the board", but that still doesnt meet code in my situation because I still have a range that has output of 120,000 BTU. Maybe I will just buy an induction. Does someone have experience with this, or installed the fantech systems, or similar, in the way I am describing without issues? We get probably 2 months where it will be close to if not freezing temps. I dont need the heat all that much. The cooling would be nice but not 20k nice. Plus I would likely just use 3 burners max most of the time and run the fan on the lowest setting. So why 6 burners? I dont know, it looks cool. Its big and its gas. I just want it. I also know that there will be added costs, so dont need a lecture on that, but lets be reasonable. I'll pay 6-8k for the entire system. That includes roughly less than 4k in unit costs (fan + MUA w heater). Would it really take $2-4 k in materials and labor to run the ducting??? (fan goes straight up out the roof, and MUA is about a 10 ft duct run--- all in the attic with an exposed ceiling at the moment). Help me make this make sense. For anyone looking for a new career, apparently there is a massive gap in the MUA residential business, you'd make a killing and be super busy.

text: I was out yesterday working around my most prosperous plant of 'Russelliana' and cleaning it out a trifle, and was thinking what a great rose it is.  'Russelliana' is listed as a hybrid Multiflora, a group that has a bad history in my garden, but then along comes this variety and blows my doubts away.  It's growing in rocky clay, sometimes very wet, and seems entirely happy.  (The wet may be advantageous:  it's a stronger plant than the other two I have growing in heavy, more droughty ground.)  My plant has been in place a dozen years of so. A warning from a seller of fruit trees strongly suggested bending new ones over and covering with four to five inches of soil. title: Floof! Leaving Reviews. | Houzz Forum
text: Do you make it a habit to leave reviews in general? For me, it depends. I generally do not leave reviews for things I buy on Amazon, unless the product is deceptively advertised or complete junk. Though typically if I get a refund for a return on said product I do not. For in person services like doctors, I have left a 5 star review one time, for my PCP, because while not a new doctor, he was new to town and starting a new practice. He really is great. A good listener, takes a lot of time with every concern, will order ANY test you want or send you to any specialist you ask for without question. I thought a good review on Google would help. So I left him one. My other doctors are well established and very busy, so I do not bother. The only time I had a really bad experience with a doctor was the surgeon I went to see about my biopsy after my mammogram. I found him to be arrogant, dismissive, and rushed. He was mid sentence when his phone rang. He answered his phone and walked out, without another word, His nurse informed me that he probably had nothing more to say. So i left. I just let it go. I just needed him to do the biopsy, I didnt need him to care. I said nothing to anyone about it. The next 2 or 3 visits with him, he was totally different. Attentive and nice, even compassionate. So maybe he was having a bad day or dealing with personal troubles. Everyone has off days. I am glad I did not complain about him. I have never left a review for a restaurant. Taste is subjective and places with bad customer service will not last long anyway, so I never saw the need. I try to help individuals with small businesses or who sell things on the side, so for Etsy or Ebay I try to make an effort to return to the site after I get the item to leave a brief positive review if the transaction and item were satisfactory. I try to refrain from leaving bad reviews. I was recently messaged by a seller on Etsy though, and I almost left a pretty bad review for her, but did not. Basically, she asked me why I had not left her a review. Didn't I like the earrings? I responded that while I did in fact like the earrings, I ordered 5 pairs from her, 2 were for gifts. And as she did not see fit to ship them for 3 weeks, the birthdays I ordered them for were past, and they had to become Christmas gifts, and I had to scramble for replacement gifts. I told her that printing a shipping label and marking the order as "shipped" was a lousy thing to do if she were going to hold the product hostage until she felt like taking her butt to the post office, and for the inconvenience, I decided to not leave a review at all, though I should probably as a warning to other people who want things that they ordered to be shipped in a timely manner. There are a couple of options for cleaning in most fabric inventories...S- solution based cleaning W- water based cleaning. IS EITHER ONE EASIER/Better for taking care of velvets? I don't think crushing is a factor...WHY? Because they'll ALL show age and wear eventually that way...(Like leather, which scratches, and darkens with skin oils etc...it's part of the distressing that people actually like...It makes it look softer, more inviting....ALSO guess what, they are selling 'distressed' velvets these days lol) There are some MUCH older threads on velvet couches (several years old) but SO MUCH has come out in the past couple years with velvets that I am not sure if they reflect the current product mix. There seem to be a couple off options: 1) Cotton 2) Cotton blend 3) Polyester blend 4) 100% poly Anyone have recommendations, experience, thoughts about performance vs non-performance velvet fabrics in a pet friendly home? title: Mixed results with meal delivery service | Houzz Forum
text: So early on this year, I was reflecting on how I might improve my life situation in 2024.  As a thought exercise, I used a technique I learned from Barbra Sher in  the book, "Wishcraft."  I thought about and described what my "ideal day" would be like.  Well . . . in my ideal day, I don't have to cook dinner, someone serves it to me and cleans up after it.  The reason is that I almost always get a second wind in the afternoon and I really resent having to stop mid project and cook dinner.   I also am getting to dislike meal planning because my husband eats what I cook for dinner, and when I ask him what he wants he almost never has any ideas, "whatever" is his stock reply, but then he rolls his eyes if I serve left overs or something vegetarian he doesn't like.  He doesn't realize that even though as a COURTESY to him I cook and eat meat, I don't like to, I prefer vegetarian food.  He thinks since vegetarianism isn't the norm, that meat eating isn't a burden or a compromise.  He has a singular perspective.  But then complains about tofu and lentils, both of which are a delicious and perfectly normal part of a vegetarian diet. Well I'm not going to get my personal vegetarian chef, but I thought maybe trying one of the meal delivery services might at least add a little fun to meal times.  I called a friend who has been doing it for years with Blue Apron, she encouraged me to try.  I chose "Dinnerly" because it was less expensive and I was not interested in meals being delivered pre-made wrapped in beaucoup plastic.  Dinnerly seemed the most local and least packaged. So far I have liked the meals a lot but am probably going to cancel.  Hubs thought the whole thing was silly and a waste of money.  I enjoyed not having to think much about dinner.  I was able to get some items I wouldn't buy in the store because I would have had to buy larger sizes and don't have the storage space.  I enjoyed the convenience of having everything pre-measured. Still, just too much plastic, although not dramatically more than the way things are mostly at a grocery store.  Try as I do, it is pretty hard to avoid plastic food containers.  About 75% of the produce was sealed in plastic.  Not all, but most.  In the store I have to use the plastic produce bags, even though I wash them and re-use some of them, so that wasn't a lot different.  Little individually packaged dry goods and sauces, as opposed to larger bulk containers, but still would be mostly plastic.  Hubs didn't much care for the vegetarian options but he is very negative.  But in the middle of the week he said he wanted chili, which was not on the menu, so we had to eat separate that night.  Weeks go by and he has no request, and then all of a sudden he wants chili with meat in it.  I get it, he just doesn't like to eat vegetarian, despite his saying otherwise.  Only once and a while, not on a regular basis.  I feel the opposite, meat is OK once and a while but not on a regular basis.  Yes of course I know how to make stuff that can just have additional meat added.  Just more cooking  for me and I don't enjoy cooking, just the eating part! Does anyone use a book that describes how to make your own vegetarian meal kits?  That was another thought I had, maybe making my own kit on Sundays.  I also thought about hiring someone to come in once a week and do meal prep for me.  Anyone ever tried that?  I think it would be hard to find someone who could do vegetarian around here.  I have a classmate who does that kind of thing, but she's a big meat eater, farm girl who does fantastic traditional foods but I would say probably not into lentils and tofu . . . I could come up with my own meal kits, but I really would love not to have to spend a lot of brain power/energy on thinking about this.  That's what I liked about Dinnerly, giving my cooking/meal planning brain a rest.  I have plenty of other things to occupy my brain right now.
